stories.title: Why Can Birds Fly?
stories.text:
Guangguang lifts a tiny paper bird. "Why can real birds fly?"

Birds have light, hollow bones—less weight to lift.

Strong chest muscles pull those wings hard.

Feathers catch the air like soft little sails.

A flap pushes air down, and the bird goes up.

Gliding rides moving air under the curved wing.

People are heavier and have no wing feathers.

Airplanes borrow the same idea with big wings.

Watch how a wing curves when a bird turns.

Push, then coast. Push, then coast again.

Birds aren't magic—they're built for the sky.

Next time you see a bird, count one careful flap.

stories.title: Why Do Cats Purr?
stories.text:
A cat curls up. Rrr-rrr. Guangguang whispers, "Tiny motor?"

Cats often purr when they feel safe and happy.

Soft petting, resting, or snuggling can start the sound.

Muscles near the voice box vibrate as the cat breathes.

Air in, air out—tiny vibes make the purr.

Some cats also purr when they need comfort.

Nervous moments may bring a quiet, steady purr too.

Purring does not mean "leave me alone."

Soft ears and a soft body usually mean the cat likes it.

Pet gently. Watch the whole cat, not only the sound.

If the cat walks away, stop and give space.

Kind hands, calm purrs—friends who listen carefully.

stories.title: Why Do Dogs Wag Their Tails?
stories.text:
A dog's tail goes swish-swish. "Always happy?" asks Guangguang.

A wagging tail is a message, not just a yes.

A loose, wide wag with a soft body often means friendly joy.

A stiff, high wag can mean unsure or on alert.

Look at ears, mouth, and how close the dog stands.

The whole body tells the story of the wag.

Friendly excitement looks bouncy and soft.

Alert feelings look taller, tighter, and careful.

Never rush a dog you do not know.

Ask a grown-up before you say hello.

Friendly wags are nice—calm hands are kinder.

Read the dog. Then share a gentle hello.

stories.title: How Do Fish Breathe Underwater?
stories.text:
Guangguang peeks at a fish tank. "No trip up for air?"

Fish pull water in through their mouths.

Then they push water out over their gills.

Gills are thin layers that take oxygen from water.

Oxygen moves into the fish's blood—quiet and steady.

Gills work like tiny underwater lungs for water.

Clean water helps fish breathe easily.

If water has little oxygen, fish can struggle.

People breathe air with lungs.

Fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water.

Different tools, but the same need: oxygen.

Watch the tank. Thank the quiet gill work.

stories.title: Why Do Dogs Pant?
stories.text:
Warm day. A dog goes pant-pant. "Hot?" asks Guangguang.

Dogs do not sweat much through skin like people.

Panting moves air quickly over tongue and mouth.

That airflow helps heat leave the body.

After a run, panting is a dog's cooler.

Sunny days can bring long, easy pant-pant too.

Shade and water help a warm dog feel better.

If panting is very hard and the dog seems weak, get help.

Find shade, offer water, and tell a grown-up.

Never leave a dog in a hot car.

Rest and water help everyone cool down.

Pant means cool-down—care keeps dogs safe.

stories.title: Why Do Bees Make Honey?
stories.text:
A bee visits a flower. "Snack time?" asks Guangguang.

Bees collect sweet nectar from blossoms.

They carry it home to the hive in tiny belly tanks.

In the hive, bees pass nectar and fan their wings.

Fanning dries water out until nectar turns thick.

That thick golden food is honey for the colony.

Honey helps bees through cold or flower-scarce days.

While bees work, pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies.

Pollen rides to other flowers and helps make seeds.

Honey is bee food first—people treat it carefully.

Watch bees from a safe distance with a grown-up.

Busy bees, sweet honey, and flowers that need friends.

stories.title: Why Are Some Animals Striped?
stories.text:
A zebra picture makes Guangguang tilt. "Fashion?"

Stripes can be more than decoration.

For a tiger in tall grass, stripes break up its shape.

Prey may not notice the outline as quickly.

For zebras in a group, many stripes can blur together.

A hunter may struggle to pick just one zebra.

Patterns match the places animals live and hide.

Spots, stripes, and colors can be survival tools.

Not every striped animal uses stripes the same way.

Science keeps learning from photos, tracks, and studies.

Next time you see stripes, ask: help or just pretty?

Patterns can be beautiful and useful at once.

stories.title: Why Did Dinosaurs Get So Big?
stories.text:
Guangguang holds a tiny toy T. rex. "School-bus big!"

Long ago, Earth had different plants and climates.

Some dinosaurs grew huge over many generations.

Big bodies can help reach high leaves for food.

Size can also help with defense in a wild world.

Growing big needs lots of food and time.

Not every dinosaur was a giant.

Many were chicken-sized or about dog-sized.

Fossils show bones, teeth, and footprints.

Scientists guess size and diet from those clues.

Movies exaggerate; fossils keep us honest.

Big or small, dinosaurs were real animals once.

stories.title: What Did T. rex Eat?
stories.text:
Guangguang shows long pointed teeth. "Salad?"

Tyrannosaurus rex had strong jaws and sharp teeth.

Those tools fit meat better than leafy salads.

It may have hunted living animals.

It may also have eaten animals already dead.

Big meat-eaters can do both kinds of feeding.

Tooth shape is a helpful clue.

Flat grinders often mean plant foods.

Sharp slicers often mean meat foods.

We learn from fossils, not movies alone.

T. rex was a powerful biter of its time.

Teeth tell stories if we look carefully.

stories.title: Why Do Whales Spout Water?
stories.text:
A whale blows a misty fountain. "Water fountain?"

Whales are mammals with lungs, not gills.

They must breathe air at the surface.

A blowhole sits on top of the head.

Warm breath whooshes out when the whale surfaces.

Cool air can turn that breath into mist.

The spout looks like water, but it is mostly breath cloud.

Then the whale breathes in and can dive again.

Different whales make different spout shapes.

Watch from a safe boat with grown-ups.

Kind watching keeps ocean friends safer.

Lungs, blowholes, and misty hellos at sea.

stories.title: Why Do Sharks Have So Many Teeth?
stories.text:
Guangguang counts cartoon shark teeth. "A hundred?"

Sharks grow many teeth in rows.

When a front tooth wears out, another can move up.

That keeps a working set for slippery food.

Lots of teeth means replaceable tools.

It does not mean a shark is "mean."

Different sharks eat different meals.

Some chase fish; some filter tiny plankton.

Healthy oceans help sharks and other sea life.

Respect wild sharks from a safe distance.

Teeth are tools that get replaced over time.

Ocean neighbors need clean, living seas.

stories.title: Why Do Camels Have Humps?
stories.text:
A camel hump looks like a backpack. "Water tank?"

A camel’s hump stores fat, not a jug of water.

Fat is energy when food is hard to find.

Deserts can be hot, dry, and scarce of snacks.

Camels also save water with clever bodies.

They handle heat and thirst better than many animals.

People once guessed humps were water bottles.

Science says: energy packs for the journey.

One-hump and two-hump camels both use fat stores.

After a hard trip, a soft hump can look leaner.

Food and rest help the energy pack refill.

Desert travelers with built-in snack backpacks.

stories.title: Why Do Owls Stay Up at Night?
stories.text:
An owl’s eyes look round and ready. "Night shift?"

Many owls hunt when nights are busy with small animals.

Mice and other snacks often move after dark.

Soft feathers help owls fly with quiet wings.

Big eyes gather dim moonlight and starlight.

Keen ears help find tiny rustling sounds.

Night tools fit night hunting.

Not every owl is strictly a night-only bird.

Some hunt at dawn or dusk too.

A hoot in the dark can mean a quiet flyer nearby.

Listen softly; give wild owls space.

Night-shift neighbors with silent wings.

stories.title: Why Do Butterflies Start as Caterpillars?
stories.text:
Guangguang peeks at a chrysalis. "Costume change?"

A butterfly's life starts as a tiny egg.

The egg hatches into a hungry little caterpillar.

The caterpillar eats leaves and grows very fast.

Then it makes a chrysalis—or soft pupa shell.

Inside the shell, the body quietly rebuilds.

Wings form. Legs change. A new shape waits.

At last, a butterfly climbs out carefully.

It waits for soft wings to dry and stiffen.

This big change is called metamorphosis.

Caterpillars and butterflies need different host plants.

A garden with the right leaves helps them thrive.

stories.title: Why Do Ants Walk in a Line?
stories.text:
Ants march in a neat line. "Parade?" asks Guangguang.

Ants leave scent trails for nest-mates to follow.

A good food find gets shared by the path they mark.

Other ants smell the trail and join the job.

Lines help many tiny workers move food efficiently.

Teamwork matters more than any one ant alone.

If a trail goes cold, ants may search new routes.

Their nest is a busy underground city of rooms.

Watch ants outdoors from a gentle distance.

Do not poke nests—ants need calm space to work.

Little insects show big cooperation every day.

Follow the scent road: science in tiny steps.

stories.title: Why Do Sea Turtles Come Ashore?
stories.text:
A turtle crawls onto sand. "Beach day?"

Many sea turtles lay eggs on sandy beaches.

They grew in the ocean but need land for nests.

A mother digs a soft pit above the tide line.

She lays eggs, covers them, then returns to sea.

Warm sand helps the eggs develop over time.

Hatchlings later race toward the bright ocean.

Lights and trash on beaches can confuse them.

Kind people keep nesting beaches dark and clean.

Never pick up wild hatchlings without experts.

Ocean homes, sandy nurseries, careful humans.

Sand, eggs, and a long swim ahead.

stories.title: Why Do Frogs Jump So Far?
stories.text:
A frog leaps. Boing! "Super legs?"

Frog back legs are long and strong.

Muscles store a springy push for takeoff.

Webbed feet help landings and swimming too.

Jumping helps frogs catch food and escape danger.

Not every hop is the same length.

Some frogs climb; some swim more than they leap.

Look at the whole frog, not only the jump.

Wet skin needs moist places to stay healthy.

Ponds and clean water help frog neighbors.

Strong legs, soft landings, careful habitats.

Boing science: push, fly, splash.

stories.title: Why Do Octopuses Have Eight Arms?
stories.text:
An octopus waves many arms. "Why eight?"

Eight arms help grab, taste, and explore.

Suckers can hold rocks, food, and tools.

Arms let an octopus open shells cleverly.

They also help crawl across the seafloor.

An octopus can squeeze through small gaps.

Soft bodies plus many arms make great explorers.

Ink and color changes help them stay safe.

Ocean rocks and reefs are favorite hideouts.

Watch gently in aquariums with grown-ups.

Eight helpers for a curious ocean mind.

Grab, taste, hide, explore.

stories.title: Why Do Penguins Huddle Together?
stories.text:
Penguins pack into a fluffy crowd. "Group hug?"

Cold winds steal heat from lonely birds.

A huddle shares warmth across many bodies.

Penguins take turns at the chilly outer edge.

Friends in the middle get a warmer break.

Huddles help eggs and chicks stay safer too.

Teamwork is survival on icy shores.

Not every penguin species huddles the same way.

Watching from afar keeps wild birds calm.

Warmth, turns, and togetherness matter here.

Cold places reward good neighbors.

Fluffy science: share the heat.

stories.title: Why Do Elephants Have Trunks?
stories.text:
An elephant trunk swings. "Super nose?"

A trunk is a nose and a helper hand together.

Elephants smell, breathe, and drink with it.

They can grab leaves and lift light objects.

Trunks spray water for cool baths.

Soft tip fingers help careful picking.

Babies practice trunk skills as they grow.

Herds use trunks in gentle hellos too.

Never tease wild elephants—give wide space.

Respect big animals with quiet watching.

Nose plus hand equals trunk power.

Smell, sip, spray, say hello.

stories.title: Why Do Giraffes Have Long Necks?
stories.text:
A giraffe stretches high. "Why so tall?"

Long necks help reach leaves other animals miss.

Tall browsing can mean extra food options.

Necks also help giraffes watch for danger far away.

Strong hearts pump blood up that long path.

Special valves help blood flow carefully.

Calves grow into their height over time.

Not every tall animal uses height the same way.

Savanna trees and giraffes fit together.

Watch quietly; wild giraffes need calm space.

High snacks, far views, careful bodies.

Tall science under the sun.

stories.title: Why Do Spiders Spin Webs?
stories.text:
A shiny web sparkles. "Art project?"

Many spiders spin silk from their bodies.

Webs can catch flying insects for food.

Different web shapes fit different hunting styles.

Silk is strong for its thin size.

Spiders may rebuild webs when weather tears them.

Not every spider waits on a big orb web.

Some hunt by chasing or hiding instead.

Most spiders are helpful neighbors for gardens.

Give them space; watch without touching webs.

Silk threads, patient hunters, tiny engineers.

Sparkle science between leaves.

stories.title: Why Do Bats Sleep Upside Down?
stories.text:
Guangguang hangs a sock by its toes. "Bats sleep upside down—why?"

Bat feet lock around a perch so hanging takes little energy.

Their legs and hips are built for dangling, not long walking.

From a hang, a bat can drop and open wings into flight fast.

Taking off from the ground is harder for many bat bodies.

Caves, trees, and quiet roofs make safe upside-down bedrooms.

Hanging high keeps bats away from many ground hunters.

They rest by day and wake to hunt insects in soft night air.

Echolocation clicks help some bats find food in the dark.

Bats are helpers: many eat mosquitoes and other pests.

Watch bats from a calm distance—never poke roosts.

Toes lock, drop, and fly: a clever upside-down bedtime.

stories.title: Why Do Zebras Have Stripes?
stories.text:
Black and white flash by. "Why stripes?" asks Guangguang.

Scientists study several helpful stripe ideas together.

Stripes may confuse biting flies that chase solid shapes.

Moving stripes can make it harder for flies to land.

In a herd, stripes may blur who begins and who ends.

That blur can make a hunter pause for a moment.

Stripes also help zebras recognize family patterns.

Each zebra's stripe map is a little different.

Open grasslands are bright—patterns matter in motion.

Zebras still need space, water, and calm watching.

Never chase wild zebras; learn from books and zoos too.

Stripes: fly tips, herd blur, and family ID—science keeps asking.

stories.title: Why Do Kangaroos Hop?
stories.text:
Guangguang bounce-bounces. "Why hop?"

Kangaroos have strong back legs and long springy feet.

Hopping stores and returns energy like a soft pogo.

Tendons stretch and snap back to help the next jump.

At travel speed, hopping can save energy on open land.

A heavy tail helps balance like a friendly third leg.

Front paws are free for soft touches and little tasks.

Joeys ride in a pouch while moms hop carefully.

Different kangaroo sizes hop in their own ways.

Give wild hoppers wide space—no chasing for fun.

Watch with a grown-up and cheer from far away.

Strong legs, spring tendons, balanced tail: hop science.

stories.title: Why Do Dolphins Click and Whistle?
stories.text:
Clicks echo in Guangguang's pretend ocean. "Why so noisy?"

Dolphins use sound to talk with friends nearby.

Whistles can be like names that help them find each other.

Clicks bounce off fish and return as soft echo maps.

That echo sense is called echolocation—seeing with sound.

Murky water is less of a problem when ears lead the way.

Pods stay close by chatting across short distances.

Playful leaps and spins often come with happy sounds.

Listening quietly teaches more than chasing boats.

Wild dolphins need calm seas and respectful space.

Learn from aquariums and nature shows with a grown-up.

Click, whistle, listen: ocean friends speak in sound.

stories.title: Why Do Fireflies Glow?
stories.text:
Tiny lights blink in the grass. "Why glow?"

Fireflies make light with a gentle chemical reaction.

The glow is cold light—little heat, lots of soft shine.

Different blink patterns help fireflies find partners.

Some patterns say hello; others say this spot is mine.

Larvae may glow too as they grow toward flashy nights.

Warm evenings after rain often bring more blinks.

City lights can hide the tiny messages—dark helps.

Cupping a firefly briefly then letting it go is kind.

Never spray chemicals where soft blinkers live.

Sit still and count flashes like a night science game.

Chemistry, patterns, and patience: backyard star bugs.

stories.title: Why Do Crabs Walk Sideways?
stories.text:
A crab skitters left. "Why sideways?" Guangguang laughs.

Many crab leg joints swing best in a side-to-side path.

Side steps fit their wide flat bodies on sand and rock.

Quick sideways dashes help them slip into tiny shelters.

Some crabs can walk forward a little, but side is smoother.

Claws up front are busy—legs behind do the travel work.

Tide pools are busy cities of sideways traffic.

Watch footprints in wet sand: little side-dash tracks.

Give crabs room; pinching claws are for crab business.

Never yank a crab from a rock hole—it needs that home.

Tide pool rules: look, learn, leave creatures in place.

Sideways isn't silly—it's joint design on the move.

stories.title: Why Do Beavers Build Dams?
stories.text:
Splash! Sticks pile up. "Why build dams?"

Beavers cut trees and pack mud to slow a stream.

The pond behind a dam makes a safer deep home zone.

Deep water hides the entrance to their lodge.

Stored branches underwater are winter snack shelves.

Dam ponds also help other animals find wet habitat.

Engineers with orange teeth reshaping the creek.

Listen for soft slap warnings on the water surface.

Leave beaver work alone—removing dams can harm homes.

Watch from a trail with a grown-up and binoculars.

Nature's builders teach patience and planning.

Stick, mud, pond, lodge: beaver town planning.

stories.title: Why Do Snakes Stick Out Their Tongues?
stories.text:
A tongue flicks softly. "Why?" asks Guangguang kindly.

Snakes smell with their tongues—not to be rude.

Tiny scent bits stick to the tongue tip.

The tongue carries smells to a special nose-inside sensor.

That sensor helps map where prey or paths might be.

Flicking gathers fresh air samples again and again.

A forked tip can compare left and right scent clues.

Snakes are shy neighbors; most want quiet space.

Never grab or tease a snake—call a grown-up if worried.

Learn safe local snakes from park rangers and books.

Curiosity is good; touching wild snakes is not.

Flick, sense, map: tongues that smell the world.

stories.title: Why Do Hummingbirds Hover?
stories.text:
Wings blur. "How do they hang in the air?" Guangguang asks.

Hummingbirds beat their wings in a special figure-eight path.

That path makes lift on both the forward and back strokes.

Most birds get lift mainly on the downstroke—hover needs both.

Tiny strong muscles power hundreds of beats each second.

Hovering lets them sip nectar while staying at the flower.

They can also fly backward and sideways for careful sips.

High-energy food from flowers fuels the busy wing work.

Garden feeders help when placed clean and high enough.

Watch softly—sudden moves can scare these tiny flyers.

Never grab a hummingbird; eyes and quiet feet are enough.

Figure-eight wings + fuel = floating flower visits.

stories.title: Why Do Polar Bears Have White Fur?
stories.text:
White fur against snow. "Camouflage?" Max asks.

Polar bear fur looks white, which helps them blend on ice.

Each hair is mostly clear and hollow like a soft tube.

Light scatters in the hollow hairs so we see white.

Under the fur, skin is dark and helps hold warmth.

Fat and fur coats keep heat in freezing winds.

Big paws spread weight on snow like soft snowshoes.

Hunting needs patience; white helps them stay less noticed.

Climate and ice changes matter a lot for their homes.

Learn and care—wild bears need distant respect always.

Never approach a polar bear; watch films and museums instead.

Hollow hairs, dark skin, thick coats: Arctic design.

stories.title: Why Is Grass Green?
stories.text:
Lawn picnic. "Why green, not purple?"

Grass leaves hold a tiny helper called chlorophyll.

Chlorophyll catches sunlight to help make food.

It reflects more green light toward our eyes.

So grass looks green while it works.

Other paints in leaves hide under that green.

In fall, some greens fade and reds show up.

Healthy grass still needs water and light.

Too little sun can make grass look pale.

Green is a working color, not just decoration.

Touch soft blades—tiny solar kitchens.

Green grass means sunlight helpers are busy!

stories.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
stories.text:
Pretend sip—blech! "Why so salty?"

Rain falls on rocks and soil inland.

Water picks up tiny mineral bits, including salt.

Rivers carry those bits toward the sea.

Ocean water keeps collecting dissolved minerals.

Sun evaporates water, but salt mostly stays behind.

Over long time, seas taste salty.

Not every lake is as salty as the ocean.

Some inland seas can be even saltier.

Salt is a traveler that settled in the big blue.

Waves splash—taste is science, not magic.

Rinse hands after beach play—salt sticks!

stories.title: Why Do Onions Make Us Cry?
stories.text:
Chop chop—then sniffles. Onion tears!

Cutting an onion breaks open tiny cells.

Those cells release sharp-smelling gases.

The gases rise and tickle your eyes.

Eyes make tears to wash the tickle away.

Tears are a helpful rinse, not sadness only.

Chilling an onion can slow the gas a bit.

Cut near a gentle fan blowing gases away.

Grown-ups may cry too—same onion chemistry.

Soup still tastes great after the sniffles.

Science in the kitchen: smell meeting eyes.

Blink, smile, keep cooking with care.

stories.title: Why Does Popcorn Pop?
stories.text:
A quiet kernel sits still on the counter. Then—POP!

Guangguang jumps. "Why does popcorn pop like that?"

Inside each hard kernel is a little water.

Heat turns that tiny water into steam.

Steam needs more room than liquid water.

Pressure builds inside the tough little shell.

Suddenly the hard shell bursts wide open.

The soft inside flips out fluffy and white.

That's the loud pop you hear and see.

If a kernel is too dry, it may not pop.

Heat and a sip of water work as a team.

Not exploding candy—just a steamy seed surprise.

stories.title: Why Do Magnets Stick to Some Things?
stories.text:
Fridge magnet sticks. "Why not wood?"

Magnets pull on iron, nickel, and some steels.

Those metals have tiny magnetic regions inside.

A magnet can line them up and hold on.

Wood, plastic, and glass usually do not stick.

They lack those ready magnetic partners.

Two magnet poles can attract or push apart.

Opposite poles pull together; same poles push.

Magnet power fades with distance.

Compasses use Earth's big magnetic field.

Stick science is selective—not magic glue.

Try fridge, keys, and a wooden spoon—compare!

stories.title: Why Do Bananas Turn Brown?
stories.text:
A yellow banana gets freckles, then brown. “Why?” asks Guangguang.

Bananas keep changing after they’re picked. A natural signal tells them to ripen. Soft enzymes break down the firm parts, and the peel’s color shifts from green to yellow to brown. Bruises brown faster where cells got squished.

Cooler air slows ripening; a warm bowl speeds it up. Brown spots can still mean sweet fruit inside—check with a grown-up if it smells okay.

So browning is ripening chemistry, not a banana “catching a cold.”

stories.title: Why Does Metal Feel Colder Than Wood?
stories.text:
Guangguang touches a metal spoon and a wooden spoon. “The metal feels colder—but are they different temperatures?”

Often they are nearly the same temperature in the room. Metal moves heat away from your fingers quickly, so your skin cools fast and you feel “cold.” Wood moves heat more slowly, so it feels warmer to the touch.

A winter metal slide can feel icy for the same reason—it steals heat from your hands fast.

So “feels colder” is about heat leaving your skin, not always about the object being frozen.

stories.title: Why Do We Hiccup?
stories.text:
Hic—! Guangguang blinks. “Why do we hiccup?”

A hiccup is a sudden squeeze of the breathing muscle under your lungs, called the diaphragm. Air pops in, and your voice box makes a tiny “hic.” Spicy food, fizzy drinks, or a big laugh can tickle that muscle.

Most hiccups stop on their own. Slow breaths and a sip of water can help. If hiccups last a long time, tell a grown-up.

So hiccups aren’t a tiny animal sneezing inside you. They’re a short glitch in a helpful breathing muscle.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Five Fingers?
stories.text:
Guangguang counts Max’s fingers. “Why five?”

Humans usually grow five digits on each hand. That layout helps us grip, pinch, and use tools. Fossils show our distant relatives also had a five-digit pattern that worked well and stuck around.

Some people are born with more or fewer digits. Bodies can vary and still be wonderful.

So five fingers aren’t a rule of the universe—they’re a useful design that evolution kept.

stories.title: Why Does Bread Get Moldy?
stories.text:
Green fuzz on bread. “Ew—why?”

Mold is a tiny living fungus. Spores float in air, land on food, and grow when it’s moist and not too cold. Bread is a cozy buffet for them.

Cool, dry, sealed storage slows mold. Fuzzy bread should be thrown away—don’t just scrape the top.

So mold isn’t magic dirt. It’s life throwing a party on leftovers.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Eyebrows?
stories.text:
Guangguang draws brows on a face. “What for?”

Eyebrows help keep sweat and rain from running straight into your eyes. They also show feelings—surprise, worry, joy—so friends can read your face.

They’re small, but busy. Without them, faces look different and eyes get dripper.

So eyebrows are rain gutters plus emotion signals.

stories.title: Why Does Ice Cream Melt?
stories.text:
A scoop sags. “Why so fast?” Max wails.

Ice cream is frozen water, fat, and sugar mixed with air. Warm air and your tongue add heat. Heat makes ice crystals turn back into liquid, so the scoop collapses into soup.

Shade and a cold bowl slow the melt. Summer sun speeds it up.

So melting is heat winning against frozen crystals—delicious, temporary art.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Hiccups After Soda?
stories.text:
Fizz! Hic! “Why now?”

Bubbly drinks can tickle your stomach and the diaphragm—the breathing muscle under your lungs. A sudden squeeze makes that tiny “hic.” Cold fizz and fast gulps make it more likely.

Slow sips help. Most hiccups pass soon.

So soda hiccups are bubbles plus a jumpy breathing muscle.

stories.title: Why Is Honey Sticky?
stories.text:
A spoon stretches a gold thread. “Why sticky?”

Honey is thick sugar syrup made by bees. Very little water remains, so sugar molecules cling and flow slowly. That thickness helps honey last a long time when sealed well.

Warmth makes honey runnier. Cold makes it stiffer.

So sticky honey is concentrated sweetness with almost no splashy water left.

stories.title: Why Do We Dream?
stories.text:
Max yawns. “Why dream?”

While you sleep, your brain stays busy. Dreams often happen in a sleep stage with rapid eye movements. Scientists think dreaming may help sort memories, practice feelings, or just be the brain’s nighttime noise.

Everyone’s dreams differ. Scary dreams can fade when you talk them out with a grown-up.

So dreams are your brain’s night theater—still mysterious, totally normal.

stories.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
stories.text:
A crescent hangs. “Is it broken?”

The Moon doesn’t really change shape. Sunlight lights different parts as the Moon orbits Earth. We see a slice, a half, or a full bright circle depending on where the Moon sits.

It’s the same rocky ball, different lighting. No cheese missing.

So moon “phases” are a spotlight show, not the Moon dieting.

stories.title: Why Do Apples Turn Brown After Cutting?
stories.text:
A slice browns. “Why?”

Cutting lets air touch apple cells. A natural chemical reaction with oxygen turns the cut surface brown. Lemon juice can slow it by changing the chemistry.

Brown isn’t always unsafe, but mushy rotten fruit should be skipped.

So apple brown is air meeting fruit chemistry—not the apple blushing.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Two Eyes?
stories.text:
Guangguang peeks with one eye. “Why two?”

Two eyes see from slightly different angles. Your brain combines the views to judge distance—handy for catching a ball or pouring milk. If one eye rests, the other still helps you see.

Depth vision is a team sport for eyeballs.

So two eyes are a built-in 3D measuring kit.

stories.title: Why Does Salt Melt Ice on Sidewalks?
stories.text:
White salt on ice. “How does that work?”

Salt lowers the freezing point of water. Ice can melt even when the air is still a bit below the normal freezing temperature. The salty water stays liquid longer.

Too much salt can bother plants and pets’ paws—grown-ups choose carefully.

So sidewalk salt is chemistry that asks ice to give up sooner.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Belly Buttons?
stories.text:
Max pokes his. “What’s this scar for?”

Before birth, a cord brought food and oxygen from mom. After birth, the cord is clamped and falls away. The belly button is the healed mark that remains.

Innies and outies are both normal. It’s a souvenir of how you grew.

So a belly button is a tiny life-history badge, not a button for clothes.

stories.title: Why Do Balloons Stick to Hair After Rubbing?
stories.text:
Rubber squeaks on hair. Then—stick! “Why?”

Rubbing moves tiny electric charges. The balloon and hair get opposite charges, so they pull together. That’s static electricity—not glue and not magic.

Dry air makes static stronger. A little moisture weakens it.

So sticky balloon tricks are invisible charge hugs.

stories.title: Why Do Leaves Fall in Autumn?
stories.text:
A red leaf drifts. “Why let go?”

As days shorten, many trees seal off leaves and stop feeding them green chlorophyll. Colors show, then leaves drop. That helps the tree save water and rest through cold or dry seasons.

Not every tree drops all leaves. Evergreens keep tough needles longer.

So autumn fall is a planned pause, not the tree giving up forever.

stories.title: Why Does Pepper Make You Sneeze?
stories.text:
Achoo! “Pepper!” Max says.

Pepper bits can tickle sensitive nerves in your nose. Your body fires a sneeze to blast the tickle out. It’s a defense reflex, not rudeness.

Keep pepper jars away from deep sniffs. Cover sneezes politely.

So pepper sneezes are your nose’s eject button for tiny irritants.

stories.title: Why Is Fire Hot?
stories.text:
Warm glow. Careful distance. “Why hot?”

Fire is a chemical reaction that releases energy as heat and light. Fuel and oxygen combine; energy that was stored in the fuel spreads out as warmth you can feel.

Never touch flames. Grown-ups handle candles and stoves.

So fire’s heat is energy escaping a fast chemical party—respect it.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Brain Freeze From Cold Drinks?
stories.text:
Ow—forehead zap! “Brain freeze?”

Very cold drinks can chill nerves in the roof of your mouth. Those nerves send a loud pain message that can feel like it’s in your forehead. It usually fades in under a minute.

Warm your tongue on the roof of your mouth. Sip slower next time.

So brain freeze is chilly nerves yelling, not your brain turning into ice.

stories.title: Why Do Cats Knead Soft Blankets?
stories.text:
Paws press-press. “Why bakery paws?”

Kneading is common in cats. Kittens press to help milk flow; grown cats may knead when cozy, claiming a soft spot with scent from their paws, or remembering kitten comfort.

It’s usually a compliment to the blanket—and to you.

So kneading is comfort behavior with kitten roots.

stories.title: Why Does Metal Rust?
stories.text:
Orange flakes on a nail. “What’s rust?”

Rust forms when iron meets water and oxygen over time. The metal changes into a crumbly orange compound. Paint and oil slow the meeting of air, water, and iron.

Stainless mixtures resist better. Dry storage helps tools last.

So rust is iron slowly combining with air and water—not orange dust falling from the sky.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Different Blood Types?
stories.text:
Guangguang shows colored stickers. “A, B, O—why?”

People’s red blood cells can carry different marker molecules. We group them into types so doctors match transfusions safely. Your type is inherited from family.

Knowing your type is useful in emergencies. Donating blood helps others—when grown-ups say you’re old enough.

So blood types are name tags on cells, discovered so medicine stays safe.

stories.title: Why Do Stars Look Pointy in Drawings?
stories.text:
Max draws spikes. “Real stars are round, right?”

Real stars are giant glowing balls. Twinkling and camera effects can make them look pointy to our eyes and in photos. Artists add points so stars pop on paper.

Space telescopes show rounder, sharper views above Earth’s blurry air.

So drawn points are art language; stars themselves are blazing spheres.

stories.title: Why Do We Yawn When Others Yawn?
stories.text:
Guangguang yawns. Max yawns. “Contagious?!”

Yawning can spread among people and some animals. Scientists think it may relate to empathy, cooling the brain, or syncing alertness in a group. We’re still learning.

You can’t always stop a contagious yawn. It’s okay—and kind of funny.

So shared yawns may be social brain echoes, not boredom contests.

stories.title: Why Does Glue Stick?
stories.text:
Two papers hug. “How does glue work?”

Wet glue flows into tiny roughness on surfaces, then hardens or dries. It grabs both sides like a microscopic handshake. Different glues use different chemistry—school glue isn’t the same as wood glue.

Use the right glue for the job, and keep caps closed.

So sticking is chemistry plus grip in the tiny hills of a surface.

stories.title: Why Do We See Our Breath in Winter?
stories.text:
A steamy puff. “Smoke?!”

Your breath holds water vapor. Cold air cools that vapor into tiny droplets you can see—like a mini cloud. It isn’t smoke or dragons, just warm moist air meeting chill.

Cover your mouth with a scarf if wind bites. Puffs mean winter physics.

So visible breath is a personal weather cloud, gone in a second.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
stories.text:
Guangguang yawns wide. "Nap attack!"

Sleep lets your body and brain recover.

While you rest, your brain sorts memories.

Your body repairs tiny wear and grows.

Kids need plenty of sleep—growing is busy work.

Dim lights tell your brain night is near.

Quiet stories help the body slow down.

Bright screens late can keep you too alert.

A calm bedtime is like a soft off-switch.

Sleep is not wasted time—it is nightly repair.

Rest well, then wake ready to play and learn.

Goodnight, little repair crew inside you.

stories.title: Why Do We Yawn?
stories.text:
A big yawn spreads. Contagious!

Scientists still study why we yawn.

It may help cool a warm busy brain.

A yawn can wake you a little bit.

It can also signal rest time to friends.

Seeing a yawn often makes you yawn too.

Humans copy soft signals—we are social.

Yawning does not always mean you are bored.

Sometimes your body wants a quick reset.

Stretch, breathe, and follow a night yawn to bed.

Day yawns can mean you need a short break.

Smile—your body just asked for a tiny reset.

stories.title: Why Do We Blink?
stories.text:
Guangguang tries not to blink. Impossible!

Your eyelids close and open—blink, blink.

Each blink spreads tears like a tiny wipe.

Tears wash away dust so eyes stay clear.

Moist eyes feel soft and comfortable.

Most blinks happen without you thinking.

Screens can make us blink less often.

Fewer blinks mean eyes feel dry and tired.

Soft, slow blinks help the surface shine.

Look far away for a gentle eye break.

Your eyelids are tiny windshield wipers.

Blink kindly—then your eyes say thank you.

stories.title: Why Does My Heart Beat?
stories.text:
Hand on chest: thump-thump. "A drum?"

Your heart is a strong muscle pump.

It pushes blood through soft tube paths.

Those paths are called blood vessels.

Blood carries oxygen and food to you.

Then blood returns to refill oxygen from lungs.

Exercise makes the heart beat faster.

Your body asks for more delivery right then.

Rest slows the beat to a calm rhythm.

A steady heartbeat is your delivery system.

Feel your pulse—gentle drum for life.

Thank your heart for every quiet thump.

stories.title: Why Do I Get a Fever?
stories.text:
Cheeks feel warm. "Broken thermostat?"

A fever often means your body is fighting germs.

A little higher heat can help defenses work.

Your immune team works hard when you feel hot.

Fevers can have other causes too.

Grown-ups decide what care you need.

Rest helps your body use its energy wisely.

Sips of water or warm drinks help a lot.

Medicine is only from a trusted adult.

Never grab pills by yourself.

Fever is a signal, not a game.

Ask for help, rest, and feel the care.

stories.title: Why Do We Wash Hands with Soap?
stories.text:
Sink time! "Why soap, not only water?" asks Guangguang.

Hands pick up tiny germs from doors, toys, and snacks.

Water alone rinses some dirt but misses oily spots.

Soap grabs oils and lifts germs so water can rinse them away.

Bubbles help soap reach cracks around nails and fingers.

Twenty seconds of scrubbing covers fronts, backs, and thumbs.

Sing a short song while you scrub to mark the time.

Rinse well, then dry—damp hands grab new germs faster.

Wash before eating and after bathroom or pet play.

Soap is a helper tool, not a scary chemical fight.

Clean hands protect you and the people you hug.

Soap + scrub + rinse + dry: tiny everyday science.

stories.title: Why Do Baby Teeth Fall Out?
stories.text:
A tooth wiggles. "Is it broken?" Guangguang worries.

Baby teeth are starters that fit a smaller jaw.

As you grow, adult teeth push up from underneath.

Roots of baby teeth shrink so the tooth can loosen.

Wiggling is often a sign the new tooth is ready.

Losing teeth makes room for bigger chewing tools.

Most kids lose teeth over several years, not all at once.

Gentle brushing still matters for wiggly and new teeth.

Do not yank hard—let the tooth leave when ready.

If a tooth hurts a lot, ask a grown-up or dentist.

A new smile grows one careful tooth at a time.

Small starters make way for grown-up chewers.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps?
stories.text:
Arms prickle. "Tiny bumps—why?" asks Guangguang.

Goosebumps happen when tiny muscles at hair roots tighten.

Cold can trigger the bumps to try to trap a little warmth.

Long ago, fluffier fur would have puffed up more.

People have thinner hair, so bumps look small now.

Big feelings—awe, scare, music—can also flip the switch.

Your body shares an old alert system with other animals.

A sweater or warm hug often smooths cold bumps away.

Scary movies can raise bumps even when you are safe.

Bumps are a signal, not a sickness by themselves.

Notice them, get cozy, and breathe if feelings feel big.

Tiny muscles, old fur trick, modern soft reminders.

stories.title: Why Do We Sneeze?
stories.text:
Ah—choo! "Why sneeze?" Guangguang asks after a tissue.

A sneeze is a fast blast that clears the nose path.

Dust, pollen, or a tickle can wake sneeze sensors.

Your body pushes air out to sweep the irritant away.

Eyes may close for a blink during the big blast.

Covering with a tissue or elbow keeps spray kinder.

Some sneezes come with colds; some are just dust.

Bright light makes a few people sneeze—a curious quirk.

If sneezes keep coming, a grown-up can help check why.

Hydration and clean air can calm a tickly nose.

Sneezes are helpers, even when they interrupt stories.

Sensors, blast, cover: nose cleanup in a flash.

stories.title: Why Do I Have a Belly Button?
stories.text:
Shirt up. "This button does nothing—why keep it?"

Before birth, a cord brought food and oxygen to you.

That cord connected to the place that is now your navel.

After birth the cord is clamped and gently falls away.

The healed spot becomes your belly button scar-soft mark.

Innies and outies are both normal shapes of healing.

The button is a reminder of how you grew, not a toy.

Keep it clean like the rest of your skin in the bath.

Doctors checked it when you were a tiny newborn.

Every person who grew that way has a belly button story.

It is quiet history written on your middle.

Cord, heal, mark: your first delivery line.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Skin?
stories.text:
"Skin is just wrapping—right?" Guangguang taps softly.

Skin is a living shield that keeps insides safely in.

It blocks many germs and dirt from easy entry.

Skin helps hold moisture so you do not dry out.

Nerves in skin tell you hot, cold, soft, and ouch.

Sweat glands help cool you when you run and play.

Melanin pigment gives a range of beautiful skin tones.

Cuts trigger a repair team of clotting and new cells.

Gentle washing and lotion keep the shield comfortable.

Sunscreen and shade protect skin on bright days.

Your largest organ works quietly every minute.

Shield, sense, cool, heal: skin does big jobs.

stories.title: Why Do Muscles Get Sore After Exercise?
stories.text:
Stairs hurt tomorrow. "Did I break my legs?"

Hard play makes tiny muscle fiber repairs begin.

Soreness often peaks a day later as rebuilding starts.

Your body reinforces muscles so next time feels easier.

This delayed ache is common after new or big efforts.

Gentle movement, water, and sleep help recovery.

Stretching softly can feel nice but is not magic alone.

Sharp sudden pain is different—tell a grown-up then.

Rest days let the rebuild finish its quiet work.

Stronger muscles are a gift from careful practice.

Soreness means remodel, not that you failed.

Work, tiny repair, stronger: workout science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Two Kidneys?
stories.text:
"Two filters—why not one?" Guangguang peeks at a diagram.

Kidneys clean blood and balance water and salts.

They make urine to carry wastes out safely.

Two kidneys give backup if one needs extra rest.

Many people live well with one healthy kidney.

Still, two give capacity for growth, play, and illness days.

Blood flows in; cleaned blood flows back out.

Drinking water helps kidneys do their quiet job.

Foods and medicines also pass through kidney care.

Protect them: helmets, seat belts, and grown-up guidance.

You cannot see them, but they work every hour.

Twin filters, backup plan, everyday clean-up crew.

stories.title: Why Does My Stomach Growl?
stories.text:
Grr-owl. Max blushes. “Why so loud?”

Your digestive tube squeezes to move food and gas along. When it’s emptier, the squeezes and air make louder gurgles. Hunger hormones can turn up the activity.

A snack can quiet it. Growls are normal, not rude on purpose.

So tummy thunder is plumbing plus air—sometimes on speakerphone.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Chickenpox Only Once Usually?
stories.text:
Dots and itchy memories. “Why once?”

After some infections, your immune system remembers the germ. Memory cells help block the same illness later. That’s why one bout can protect you for years—vaccines teach memory safely without the full disease.

Follow doctor advice on vaccines and itchy care.

So “only once” is often your immune library remembering the culprit.

stories.title: Why Do Babies Have Soft Spots on Their Heads?
stories.text:
Gently—Guangguang shows a doll. “Soft spot?”

Babies’ skull bones aren’t fully fused. Soft spots (fontanelles) let the head pass through birth and give the brain room to grow. They usually close as bones meet over months and years.

Be gentle. Soft doesn’t mean fragile if handled with care.

So soft spots are growth panels on a brand-new skull.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Saliva?
stories.text:
Max chews a cracker. “Why spit in my mouth?”

Saliva wets food so you can taste and swallow. It starts breaking down some starches and washes teeth. Without it, eating feels like sandpaper.

Dry mouth needs water—and sometimes a dentist’s tip.

So saliva is free sauce, cleaner, and first digester in one.

stories.title: Why Does My Heart Beat Faster When I Run?
stories.text:
Thump-thump faster! “Why race?”

Running muscles need more oxygen and fuel. Your heart pumps quicker to deliver blood. Breathing speeds up too. After rest, rates calm down.

A very odd heartbeat feeling should be told to a grown-up.

So a faster beat is express delivery for busy muscles.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Earwax?
stories.text:
Guangguang pretends to clean tiny ears—gently. “Wax?”

Earwax traps dust and bugs, and it helps keep the canal from getting too dry. It slowly works its way out. Cotton swabs can push wax deeper—ask a grown-up about safe cleaning.

A little wax is healthy armor.

So earwax is sticky security, not dirt you must dig out every day.

stories.title: Why Do Fingernails Grow?
stories.text:
Clip clip. “Why keep growing?”

Nails protect fingertip bones and help pick up tiny things. New nail material forms under the skin at the base and slowly pushes forward. Toes do the same, usually slower.

Trim carefully. Biting nails can invite germs.

So nails are living shields on a slow conveyor belt.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Allergies?
stories.text:
Achoo near pollen. “Allergy?”

An allergy is the immune system overreacting to something usually harmless, like pollen or certain foods. It releases chemicals that cause sniffles, itch, or worse.

Serious breathing trouble needs emergency help. Mild sniffles still deserve grown-up plans.

So allergies are false alarms with real symptoms—know your triggers.

stories.title: Why Do We Shiver When Cold?
stories.text:
Brr—shake shake. “Why shiver?”

Shivering is quick muscle jerks that make extra heat. Your brain turns it on when you’re chilled. Goosebumps try to fluff hair for warmth—more useful for furry animals.

Warm clothes beat long shivering. Come inside.

So shivers are your body’s emergency furnace switch.

stories.title: Why Do Kids Grow So Fast Sometimes?
stories.text:
Max’s pants shrink. “Growth spurt?”

Bones lengthen at growth plates near the ends. Hormones and good food, sleep, and play fuel spurts. Timing differs—friends may shoot up on different calendars.

Doctors track height on charts. Sudden pain needs a check.

So growing fast is a scheduled construction boom in your skeleton.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Vaccines?
stories.text:
A tiny poke. “Why?”

Vaccines teach your immune system to recognize a germ safely. Later, if the real germ arrives, memory cells respond faster. That protects you and neighbors who can’t get shots.

Scientists test vaccines carefully. Ask your doctor what’s right for you.

So vaccines are practice drills for your body’s defense team.

stories.title: Why Does the Moon Follow Us?
stories.text:
On a car ride, the Moon seems to tag along.

Guangguang asks, "Is the Moon chasing us?"

Nearby trees zoom past the window fast.

The Moon is very, very far away.

Far things seem to move slowly beside you.

So the Moon looks like a friendly follower.

It isn't jogging after the car at all.

The Moon orbits Earth on its own path.

Distance and perspective play this cozy trick.

Many towns see the same bright Moon tonight.

Not a chase—just space looking close.

Wave hello. The Moon keeps its quiet watch.

stories.title: Why Do Stars Twinkle?
stories.text:
Stars wink above. "Blinking on purpose?"

Starlight travels a very long way to Earth.

It passes through moving layers of air.

Air bends the light a tiny bit, again and again.

To our eyes, the star seems to dance and wink.

Planets look steadier—they are closer bright disks.

Twinkle is Earth's air, not the star flipping a switch.

On a still clear night, winks can look softer.

City haze may make twinkles look busier.

Astronauts above the air see stars shine steady.

So twinkle means: light plus our restless sky.

Next clear night, watch one star gently wink.

stories.title: Why Is the Sun So Bright?
stories.text:
Sunshine pours across the room. "Ow—bright!"

The Sun is a star—our closest one.

Inside, hot gases release enormous energy.

Light and warmth race outward in every direction.

Earth catches only a tiny share of that light.

Even a tiny share is enough to light our day.

Never stare straight at the Sun—it can hurt eyes.

Use shade, hats, and sideways glances outdoors.

Sunset glow is sunlight traveling a longer path.

Night comes when our side turns away from the Sun.

Bright does not mean small—our star is huge.

Thank the Sun, then play in safe soft light.

stories.title: Why Is There No Sound in Space?
stories.text:
Clap in a pretend spacesuit. Total silence!

Sound needs something to travel through.

Usually that something is air, water, or solid stuff.

Tiny pushes pass along as a wave we hear.

Space between worlds is mostly empty of air.

With almost no air, sound waves have nowhere to go.

That is why space feels so quiet in stories.

Inside a spaceship, air lets voices work again.

On Earth, air is the everyday sound highway.

Put a bell under a jar and pump air out—quieter.

No air highway means no ordinary clap-sound.

Quiet space, noisy Earth—same science, different room.

stories.title: Why Do Rockets Need Fire?
stories.text:
A toy rocket waits. "Where's the whoosh?"

Rockets push hot gas out the bottom very fast.

Push gas one way, and the rocket goes the other way.

That push-and-go idea is how rockets climb.

The bright flame is burning fuel making fast gas.

Fire here means energy turning into a strong push.

In space there is no road—only this push matters.

Wings need air; rockets can work without wings.

Real launches are loud, carefully planned, and grown-up jobs.

Toy whooshes are pretend—never play with real fire.

Gas out the back, rocket up the front—pair of forces.

Whoosh science: push down, rise up!

stories.title: Why Do We See Only One Side of the Moon?
stories.text:
The Moon’s face looks familiar every night. “Does it spin?”

The Moon does rotate, but it takes about the same time to spin once as to go once around Earth. That match is why we mostly see the same side from the ground. The far side exists—spacecraft have photographed it.

Phases change how sunlight hits the near side. Same face, different lighting. The Moon keeps a steady hello.

stories.title: Why Are There Craters on the Moon?
stories.text:
Guangguang points at round dents. “Potholes?”

Long ago, rocks from space hit the Moon hard and left bowl-shaped craters. The Moon has almost no air or weather to wear those marks away, so many craters stay sharp for ages.

Earth gets hits too, but air, water, plants, and time smooth many scars. The Moon’s face is a history book written in circles.

stories.title: What Is a Planet?
stories.text:
Guangguang spins a blue marble. “Planet?”

A planet is a big round world that orbits a star—like Earth around the Sun. Planets are much smaller than stars and don’t make their own blazing starlight the way the Sun does. Our solar system has rocky planets and giant gas planets.

Moons orbit planets. Asteroids are smaller rocky leftovers. Learning the difference helps you map the neighborhood of space.

stories.title: Why Does Earth Spin?
stories.text:
Day turns to night. “Who flipped the light switch?”

Earth spins like a top. The side facing the Sun has daytime; the side turned away has nighttime. One full spin is about 24 hours—our day. Earth also travels around the Sun, which helps make seasons with the tilt of Earth’s axis.

We don’t feel the spin because everything around us spins too, smoothly. Sunrise is Earth turning toward the Sun again.

stories.title: How Many Planets Are in Our Solar System?
stories.text:
Guangguang lines up toy worlds. “Count!”

Our solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. They all orbit the Sun. Dwarf planets like Pluto are smaller worlds with their own stories.

Astronomers update labels as they learn more. Eight big planets orbit our star—and Earth is the one with oceans, air, and you.

stories.title: What Is a Comet?
stories.text:
A fuzzy visitor streaks. “Comet?”

A comet is a dirty snowball of ice, dust, and rock. Near the Sun, ice turns to gas and dust streams into a glowing tail that always points away from the Sun’s push.

Comets orbit on long paths. They aren’t burning airplanes.

So a comet is a sunny thaw parade of ancient ice and dust.

stories.title: What Is an Asteroid?
stories.text:
Rocky dots between planets. “Asteroids?”

Asteroids are rocky leftover pieces from the solar system’s youth, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Some are small as cars; others are much bigger. Spacecraft have visited a few.

They’re not stars. They shine by reflecting sunlight.

So asteroids are leftover building blocks floating in a rocky belt.

stories.title: Why Is Mars Red?
stories.text:
A rusty marble. “Why red?”

Mars soil has lots of iron oxide—rust. Dust in the air can make the whole planet look reddish. It’s cold and dry compared with Earth, with polar ice and giant volcanoes from long ago.

Rovers study its rocks for clues about past water.

So Mars wears a rusty coat, not red paint.

stories.title: What Is the Milky Way?
stories.text:
A milky band in a dark sky. “Our galaxy?”

The Milky Way is the huge star city we live in—billions of stars, gas, and dust in a flat spiral. From Earth we see it edge-on as a pale river of light.

Other galaxies shine far beyond. Telescopes are our ships.

So the Milky Way isn’t spilled milk—it’s home on a cosmic scale.

stories.title: Why Do Astronauts Float in Space?
stories.text:
Guangguang pretends to float. “Zero gravity?”

In orbit, astronauts and their ship are both falling around Earth together. Because everything falls at the same rate, they feel weightless—like continuous freefall without hitting the ground.

It’s not that gravity vanished. Earth still pulls.

So floating is shared falling in circles—space ballet with science.

stories.title: What Is a Black Hole?
stories.text:
A dark circle in a diagram. “Scary?”

A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that light can’t escape from inside a boundary called the event horizon. They form from very massive stars collapsing, among other ways.

They don’t roam eating everything nearby like monsters. Orbits can be stable far out.

So black holes are extreme gravity sinks—studied carefully, not bedtime villains.

stories.title: Why Is Venus So Hot?
stories.text:
A bright morning star. “Hotter than Mercury?”

Venus has a thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere that traps heat—a runaway greenhouse. Surface temperatures are oven-hot, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

Telescopes and probes study its clouds from a safe distance.

So Venus heat is a thick blanket problem, not just “nearness.”

stories.title: What Are Saturn’s Rings Made Of?
stories.text:
Sparkly rings. “Ice?”

Saturn’s rings are countless chunks of ice and rock—some tiny, some boulder-sized—orbiting in thin sheets. Moonlets and gravity sculpt gaps and waves.

They look solid from far away. Up close, they’re a glittering traffic jam.

So rings are icy rubble highways, not solid hoops.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Seasons?
stories.text:
Summer sweat, winter coats. “Why seasons?”

Earth’s axis tilts. As we orbit the Sun, one hemisphere leans toward sunlight for warmer months while the other leans away. Distance to the Sun changes a little, but tilt drives seasons.

Equator seasons differ from poles. Calendar festivals follow the tilt dance.

So seasons are a tilted Earth pirouette around the Sun.

stories.title: What Is the International Space Station?
stories.text:
A metal butterfly in orbit. “ISS?”

The International Space Station is a lab where astronauts from many countries live and work while circling Earth about every 90 minutes. They study science in microgravity and test life in space.

Cargo ships bring food and experiments. It’s a cooperative outpost.

So the ISS is a shared science home in freefall around our planet.

stories.title: Why Do Meteors Streak?
stories.text:
A quick scratch of light. “Shooting star?”

A meteor is a space rock heating and glowing as it races through Earth’s air. Most are tiny and burn up. If a piece lands, it’s called a meteorite.

Wish if you like—the physics still happens either way.

So meteor streaks are air friction light shows from visiting pebbles.

stories.title: What Is a Light-Year?
stories.text:
Guangguang draws a ruler across stars. “Light-year?”

A light-year measures distance: how far light travels in one year—about 9.5 trillion kilometers. Stars are so far that ordinary miles feel silly.

It isn’t a length of time. It’s a long cosmic measuring stick.

So light-years turn huge space into numbers we can say out loud.

stories.title: Why Does the Sun Rise in the East?
stories.text:
Morning gold. “Always east?”

Earth spins west to east. From the ground, the Sun seems to climb in the east and set in the west. The Sun isn’t racing around us each day—we’re the ones turning.

Poles and seasons tweak the path. Compasses still help hikers.

So sunrise direction is Earth’s spin painted on the sky.

stories.title: What Are Constellations?
stories.text:
Dot-to-dot bears and hunters. “Real groups?”

Constellations are patterns people imagined by connecting stars as seen from Earth. The stars in a pattern may not be close to each other in space—just lined up from our viewpoint.

Cultures drew different sky stories. Astronomers still use the names as maps.

So constellations are sky storytelling overlays on real distant suns.

stories.title: Why Do Shadows Follow Us?
stories.text:
Guangguang spins. The shadow spins too!

A shadow appears when something blocks light.

Light hits you; a dark shape falls behind.

Move left—the blocked spot moves left.

That's why the shadow seems to follow.

Move the lamp, and shadows stretch or shrink.

At noon the Sun is high; shadows stay short.

Later, long shadows walk across the ground.

Soft light makes fuzzy edges; hard light looks sharp.

Shadows are light's quiet footprints.

No feet of their own—just blocked brightness.

Dance once. Your shadow dances with you.

stories.title: Why Does Ice Melt?
stories.text:
An ice cube drips. "Disappearing act!"

Ice is water frozen into a solid shape.

Heat gives tiny bits of water more energy.

They slip free of the stiff ice pattern.

Then ice becomes liquid water you can pour.

Warm air can melt a cube on the table.

Warm hands melt ice even faster.

Sunlight adds heat on a bright day too.

Melting is not vanishing into nothing.

It is water changing form—solid to liquid.

Freeze it again and water can become ice.

Same water, different costume—cool science!

stories.title: Why Do Soap Bubbles Float?
stories.text:
A bubble drifts up, then pops!

A bubble is a thin soap-water skin.

Inside the skin is a pocket of air.

Soap makes that skin stretchy and strong.

Warm air inside can help it lift a bit.

Gentle breezes can carry bubbles along.

Gravity still pulls, so they do not fly forever.

As the skin dries, it gets thinner.

When it thins too much—pop!

Bubbles teach thin films and air together.

Sparkle colors dance on the soap skin.

Blow softly, watch, then smile at the pop.

stories.title: Why Do Balloons Float Up?
stories.text:
A helium balloon tugs the string skyward.

Helium is lighter than the air around us.

A balloon full of helium weighs less.

Less than the same-sized blob of regular air.

Denser air pushes up, so the balloon rises.

It is a bit like wood floating on water—but in air.

Regular breath balloons usually fall down.

Your breath is not lighter than outside air.

Hold strings gently when you walk outside.

Let balloons go only where it is safe.

And only where grown-ups say it is allowed.

Light gas, gentle hands, happy sky tug!

stories.title: Why Do Some Things Float?
stories.text:
A leaf rides a puddle; a pebble sinks.

Floating depends on density—how packed stuff is.

Shape matters too, not only weight.

If something pushes aside heavy water, it can float.

The water it moves can weigh more than the object.

Boats use hollow shapes to displace lots of water.

That is why a big empty boat can float.

Heavy metal can float as a boat shape.

But the same metal as a tight ball may sink.

Shape and density work as a team.

Try a leaf, a pebble, and a toy boat.

Watch who rides—and who takes a dive!

stories.title: Why Can We See Ourselves in Mirrors?
stories.text:
Guangguang waves; the glass waves back.

A mirror’s smooth surface reflects light in an orderly way. Light from your face bounces to your eyes, so you see an image. Ordinary walls scatter light messily; mirrors bounce it neatly.

Left and right look swapped in the usual way mirrors work. It’s geometry with shine.

stories.title: What Makes a Plane Fly?
stories.text:
A plane lifts off. “How?”

Airplane wings are shaped so air moving over them helps create lift—an upward push. Engines move the plane forward so air flows fast over the wings. Pilots and flaps adjust for takeoff and landing.

Birds use flapping and shape; planes use engines and fixed wings. Same sky, different toolkits.

stories.title: How Does a Simple Wheel Help?
stories.text:
Guangguang rolls a toy car. Smooth!

Wheels turn sliding friction into rolling motion, which is usually easier. Axles hold wheels so carts and bikes can carry loads with less effort than dragging.

From scooters to suitcases, wheels save energy. A round idea that still moves the world.

stories.title: Why Do Boats Float?
stories.text:
A toy boat sits high. “Heavy boats float—how?”

Floating happens when water pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the water the boat pushes aside. A boat’s shape spreads weight over enough water. A solid steel cube may sink; a steel boat hull can float.

Holes that flood the hull spoil the trick. Life jackets help people float too.

So floating is a push-up contest between object and water.

stories.title: Why Do Rubber Bands Snap Back?
stories.text:
Twang! “Why bounce back?”

Rubber’s long molecules can stretch and then pull toward their relaxed shape. That springiness stores energy when you pull and returns it when you let go—until the band breaks.

Don’t aim bands at faces. Physics is cool; safety is cooler.

So snap-back is molecular springs doing yoga.

stories.title: Why Do Bike Gears Help Hills?
stories.text:
Pedal grind. “Gears?”

Gears change how turning force and speed trade off. A low gear makes pedaling easier uphill but slower. A high gear covers ground faster on flats with more effort per turn.

Chains transfer the spin. Oil and care keep rides smooth.

So gears are mechanical translators between your legs and the hill.

stories.title: Why Do Speakers Make Sound?
stories.text:
Music shakes air. “How?”

A speaker cone moves back and forth, pushing air into waves your ears hear as sound. Electricity and magnets drive the motion following the music signal.

Louder means bigger pushes. Ears need breaks from blasting volume.

So speakers are careful air shakers writing sound waves.

stories.title: Why Do Fridges Stay Cold Inside?
stories.text:
Cold lettuce. Warm kitchen. “How?”

A fridge pumps heat from inside to the coils on the back or bottom using a special fluid cycle. It doesn’t make “coldness”—it moves heat out and keeps the door sealed.

Stuffing it full without airflow can weaken cooling. Keep the door shut.

So a fridge is a heat-moving machine with a chilly closet.

stories.title: Why Do Straws Make Drinking Easier?
stories.text:
Slurp. “Vacuum?”

When you suck, you lower air pressure in the straw. Higher outside pressure pushes the drink up toward your mouth. You’re not magically lifting with pure willpower—air helps.

Pinch the straw and flow stops. Physics in a sip.

So straws hitch a ride on air-pressure differences.

stories.title: Why Do Flashlights Need Batteries?
stories.text:
Click—beam. “Why batteries?”

Batteries store chemical energy and release it as electric current. The current heats a filament or powers LEDs to make light. Without a power source, the circuit is just dark metal.

Rechargeables can be reused many times. Recycle batteries properly.

So batteries are portable energy snacks for electrons.

stories.title: Why Do Bridges Have Triangles?
stories.text:
Steel triangles rise. “Why that shape?”

Triangles are strong and stable. Push on a triangle’s corner and the sides share the force without easily collapsing the way a floppy square might. Engineers use trusses of triangles for long spans.

Beauty and strength can team up. Design follows physics.

So bridge triangles are geometry armor against bending and swaying.

stories.title: Why Do Matches Light When Scratched?
stories.text:
Scratch—flame. Grown-up only. “How?”

Friction heat starts a chemical reaction in the match head. Special chemicals catch fire more easily than wood alone. Safety matches need the box strip.

Kids don’t light matches. Ask a grown-up for campfire rules.

So a match scratch turns rubbing heat into a tiny controlled fire starter.

stories.title: Why Do Sunglasses Help?
stories.text:
Bright glare. Dark lenses. “Just fashion?”

Good sunglasses cut harsh light and can block invisible ultraviolet rays that stress eyes over time. Polarized lenses tame bounce glare from water and roads.

Cheap dark plastic without UV protection can make pupils open wide—ask for real UV-blocking pairs.

So sunglasses are eye shade with science, not only cool looks.

stories.title: Why Do Clocks Tick?
stories.text:
Tick-tock. “Why the sound?”

Many clocks move gears in tiny steps. Escapement parts catch and release, making the tick. Quartz clocks use a vibrating crystal; the tick can be a speaker click copying the rhythm.

Timekeeping is controlled wiggles counted carefully.

So ticks are audible footsteps of a counting machine.

stories.title: Why Do Microwaves Heat Food Fast?
stories.text:
Beep. Steam. “How so quick?”

Microwave ovens make waves that jostle water molecules in food, producing heat inside—not only from the outside in like a regular oven. Metal and some containers are unsafe inside; follow the manual.

Stirring helps even heating. Hot spots can burn tongues.

So microwaves are water-molecule dance floors in a metal box.

stories.title: Why Do Parachutes Slow Falls?
stories.text:
Silk umbrella blooms. “Why safer?”

A parachute catches air, making a big drag force upward against the fall. More area means more air resistance, so the person descends slower than a free fall.

Skydiving needs training. Toy parachutes show the idea safely indoors.

So parachutes buy time by hugging a lot of air.

stories.title: Why Do Locks Need Keys?
stories.text:
Click. Door opens. “How?”

A key’s jagged edge lifts pins inside the lock to a matching height so the cylinder can turn. Wrong keys leave pins blocking. It’s a tiny 3D puzzle.

Digital locks use codes instead of teeth. Keep spare keys safe.

So keys are portable answers to a pin puzzle in metal.

stories.title: Why Do Fans Cool Us If They Don’t Make Cold Air?
stories.text:
Whirr. “Air isn’t icy—why cooler?”

Fans move air across your skin so sweat evaporates faster, carrying heat away. The air temperature may be the same; you feel cooler because heat leaves your body quicker.

In a sealed empty room with no people, a fan mostly just stirs air.

So fan “cool” is evaporating sweat express, not a fridge wind.

stories.title: Why Do Velcro Stick and Peel?
stories.text:
Rrrrip. “How?”

Velcro pairs tiny hooks with tiny loops. Pressing hooks catch loops; peeling unhooks them with that famous sound. Inspired by burrs stuck on clothes after a walk.

Dirt fills loops and weakens grip—clean when fuzzy fails.

So Velcro is miniature grappling hooks taught by nature’s burrs.

stories.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
stories.text:
Guangguang looks up. Blue forever!

Sunlight holds many colors mixed together.

Air molecules scatter blue light the most.

Red light scatters less on its way.

Looking away from the Sun, more blue reaches our eyes.

That is why daytime sky looks blue.

Near the Sun, light can look brighter white-gold.

Space looks black—there is almost no air there.

Without air, light does not scatter the same way.

Earth's air paints our blue ceiling.

Same sunlight, special sky paint.

Next sunny day, thank the tiny air helpers.

stories.title: Why Is the Sunset Red?
stories.text:
Evening turns peach and red.

At sunset, sunlight travels through more air.

Blue light scatters out of the long path.

Reds and oranges travel farther to your eyes.

Dust and clouds can deepen the colors.

Same Sun—longer path, warmer colors.

Morning sunrise can wear similar warm coats.

City haze may make reds look extra deep.

Clean air still makes soft peach evenings.

Sunsets are physics wearing a pretty coat.

Watch safely—never stare hard at the Sun.

Wave goodnight to the warm sky.

stories.title: Why Does It Rain?
stories.text:
Drops tap the window. Tap tap!

Warm air lifts invisible water vapor up.

High up, the air cools.

Tiny droplets gather into clouds.

Droplets grow heavier and heavier.

Gravity pulls them down as rain.

Rain waters plants and thirsty soil.

Rain helps fill rivers and lakes.

Too much rain can make puddle floods.

Too little rain makes dry, thirsty days.

Weather is Earth's water on the move.

Listen—rain is the sky sharing a drink.

stories.title: Why Does Thunder Follow Lightning?
stories.text:
Flash first… then comes the boom.

Lightning is a giant spark in the sky.

The spark heats air incredibly fast.

Hot air expands in a sudden shock.

That shock is the sound we call thunder.

Light races much faster than sound.

So we see the flash before we hear the rumble.

Counting seconds after a flash can hint distance.

But the safe rule is simpler.

If you hear thunder, head indoors.

Go with a grown-up. Stay cozy and dry.

Storm science and storm safety stay together.

stories.title: Why Does It Snow?
stories.text:
Soft flakes fall. Quiet white!

When clouds are cold enough, water can freeze.

Ice crystals begin to grow.

Crystals stick together into flakes.

Flakes drift down if the air stays cold.

If air is too warm, flakes may melt to rain.

Every flake grows with a pattern.

No two flake journeys are identical.

Snow is winter's quiet rain of crystals.

Snow can blanket soil and sleep seeds.

Boots, hats, and gentle play keep toes warm.

Catch one flake—then smile at winter science.

stories.title: Why Do Rainbows Appear?
stories.text:
After a shower, colors arc across the sky.

Guangguang points. "Where did that bow come from?"

Sunlight slips into tiny raindrops.

Inside each drop, light bends and reflects.

Different colors bend by different amounts.

Red, orange, yellow—then green to violet.

You need sun behind you and drops ahead.

The bow isn't a road you can walk on.

It's light's geometry painted in water.

Move a little; the rainbow seems to move too.

Same sunshine, same drops—new place to stand.

After rain, look opposite the Sun and smile.

stories.title: Why Does the Wind Blow?
stories.text:
Leaves skitter. Whoosh.

Sun warms some places more than others. Warm air rises; cooler air slides in to take its place. That moving air is wind. Land, sea, and mountains steer the flow.

Gentle breezes cool us; strong winds need caution. Wind is air with somewhere to go.

stories.title: Why Do Clouds Look Fluffy?
stories.text:
Cotton castles. “Why fluffy?”

Many fair-weather clouds are heaps of tiny water droplets or ice crystals clustered where rising moist air cools. Sunlight scatters from countless droplets, making bright white puff shapes.

Clouds can also look flat or streaky depending on winds aloft. Fluffy is just one style.

So fluff is light bouncing off a crowd of tiny droplets.

stories.title: Why Do We See Lightning Before Thunder?
stories.text:
Flash—then boom. “Why delay?”

Light races far faster than sound. You see the spark almost instantly; thunder’s rumble needs time to travel. Counting seconds between flash and boom estimates distance.

Stay indoors in storms. Metal and tall trees are risky shelters.

So the gap is a race result: light laps sound.

stories.title: What Is Fog?
stories.text:
Gray hug on the road. “Ground cloud?”

Fog is a cloud touching the ground—tiny water droplets floating in cool, moist air. Drivers slow down because droplets scatter headlights.

Fog often fades when sun warms the air. Listen for horns in thick fog.

So fog is a cloud that decided to visit street level.

stories.title: Why Do Deserts Get Cold at Night?
stories.text:
Scorching day, chilly night. “Why swing?”

Dry desert air and clear skies let heat escape quickly after sunset. Without thick humidity or clouds to blanket the ground, temperatures can plunge.

Pack layers for desert trips. Day and night are different worlds.

So desert nights cool fast because the sky leaves the door open.

stories.title: Why Do Hurricanes Spin?
stories.text:
A swirl on the map. “Why spin?”

Big storms feel Earth’s rotation. That effect helps organize winds into a spin—opposite directions in northern and southern hemispheres. Warm ocean water fuels the engine.

Forecasts help people prepare. Never chase storms for fun.

So hurricane spin is heat plus Earth’s turning, organized into a dangerous wheel.

stories.title: What Is Hail?
stories.text:
Ice peas bounce. “Frozen rain?”

Hail grows when thunderstorm updrafts loft water drops into very cold air. Layers of ice build until the stone falls. Bigger storms can toss bigger hail.

Cars and gardens dislike hail. Sturdy shelter is wise.

So hail is a thunderstorm’s ice factory, not winter snow.

stories.title: Why Is the Sky Dark at Night?
stories.text:
Stars on black. “Where did blue go?”

At night our side of Earth faces away from the Sun. Without sunlight scattering in the air toward us, the sky looks dark, and distant stars can shine through.

City lights can wash stars out. Dark parks show more sparkle.

So night dark is Earth’s shadow side, not the universe turning off.

stories.title: Why Do Puddles Disappear?
stories.text:
Morning puddle, noon dry. “Where’d it go?”

Water evaporates into invisible vapor when air and sun provide energy. Wind speeds it up. The puddle didn’t vanish into another dimension—it joined the air.

Bigger puddles last longer. Shade slows drying.

So disappearing puddles are slow-motion steam without the teapot whistle.

stories.title: What Is Humidity?
stories.text:
Sticky air. “Humidity?”

Humidity measures how much water vapor the air holds. High humidity makes sweat evaporate slowly, so you feel muggy. Low humidity can dry lips and static-charge hair.

Weather apps report it. Fans help when air is moist and still.

So humidity is the air’s invisible water load.

stories.title: Why Do Weather Maps Use Colors?
stories.text:
Blob of green and red. “What’s that?”

Colors show rain strength, temperatures, or radar echoes so your eyes grasp patterns fast. Green might mean lighter rain; yellow and red heavier—keys explain each map.

Maps forecast; windows confirm. Dress for the color story.

So weather colors are visual shortcuts for busy data.

stories.title: Why Does Dew Form on Grass?
stories.text:
Morning sparkles. “Overnight rain?”

Clear nights cool the ground. Air near the grass can cool until water vapor condenses into droplets—dew. It isn’t always from clouds raining.

Shoes get wet on purpose. Dew dries as day warms.

So dew is nighttime condensation jewelry on leaves.

stories.title: What Causes a Drought?
stories.text:
Cracked earth. “No rain?”

A drought is a long stretch of less water than usual for plants, rivers, and people. Causes include stubborn weather patterns and sometimes human water use. Conservation helps communities cope.

Follow local water rules. Lawns can wait; drinking water matters more.

So droughts are water budgets gone thin for too long.

stories.title: Why Do Weather Balloons Go Up?
stories.text:
A big balloon lifts gadgets. “Why?”

Weather balloons carry sensors that measure temperature, humidity, and pressure as they rise. Radios send data that help forecasts. When balloons burst high up, parachutes bring instruments down.

They’re science messengers, not party balloons.

So weather balloons are flying notebooks for the sky’s layers.

stories.title: Why Is Snow Quiet?
stories.text:
Soft footsteps. “Why hush?”

Fresh snow has lots of air pockets that soak up sound waves. Cities sound muffled after a blizzard. When snow melts or packs hard, the hush fades.

Enjoy the quiet—then shovel with a grown-up’s plan.

So snow quiet is acoustic foam made of frozen fluff.

stories.title: What Is the Jet Stream?
stories.text:
A fast ribbon on the forecast. “Jet stream?”

Jet streams are swift air currents high up that steer weather systems. Planes sometimes ride them to save time. They wiggle and shift with seasons.

They’re invisible rivers of wind, not airplane-only highways.

So the jet stream is a sky freeway for storms and jets.

stories.title: Why Do Windows Fog on Cold Days?
stories.text:
Steamy glass. “Fog inside?”

Warm moist indoor air hits cold glass. Water condenses into tiny droplets—fog on the pane. Wiping helps; a little ventilation can too.

It’s the same idea as breath on a mirror.

So foggy windows are indoor clouds starting on cold glass.

stories.title: Why Do Seasons Feel Different by the Ocean?
stories.text:
Coast vs inland. “Milder?”

Oceans heat and cool slowly, buffering nearby air. Coasts often have milder winters and cooler summers than deep inland places at the same latitude. Breezes carry that influence ashore.

Pack layers for beach trips anyway—wind can bite.

So oceans are giant temperature shock absorbers for coastal weather.

stories.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
stories.text:
Autumn trees wear red and gold coats.

Green comes from chlorophyll making food.

In fall, many trees slow that green work.

Chlorophyll fades, and other colors show.

Yellows and oranges were hiding underneath.

Some reds form as sugars change in cool air.

Shorter days signal leaves to prepare.

A gentle leaf scar seals where the leaf lets go.

Fallen leaves can feed the soil later.

Not every tree turns the same rainbow.

Fall color is chemistry wearing a costume.

Catch one leaf—then smile at the season.

stories.title: Why Do Volcanoes Erupt?
stories.text:
A mountain with a soft puff sits in a drawing.

Deep Earth can be hot enough to melt rock.

Melted rock is called magma.

Magma can find a path upward through cracks.

When it reaches the surface, we call it lava.

Gas bubbles help push magma up sometimes.

An eruption is Earth letting pressure out.

Some eruptions are gentle; some are stronger.

Scientists watch volcanoes to keep people safe.

Never visit a real volcano without grown-ups and rules.

Volcanoes build new land over long time.

Hot rock, rising paths, careful respect.

stories.title: What Makes an Earthquake?
stories.text:
A storybook floor wiggles softly underfoot.

Earth's outer shell has big pieces called plates.

Plates move very slowly all the time.

Sometimes stuck edges suddenly slip.

That slip sends shaking waves through the ground.
