We feel those waves as an earthquake.

Most quakes are small; some are stronger.

Buildings in quake places use special designs.

Drop, cover, and hold on if grown-ups say practice.

Earthquakes are plate motion, not monsters.

Science helps us prepare and stay calmer.

Steady feet, ready plan, soft courage.

stories.title: Why Do Oceans Have Tides?
stories.text:
Beach water creeps up the sand, then back.

The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans.

Water bulges a little toward the Moon.

Another bulge forms on the opposite side too.

As Earth turns, those bulges sweep along shores.

We see high tide and low tide.

The Sun's pull adds a smaller tide effect.

When Sun and Moon line up, tides can be bigger.

Tide pools appear when water goes out.

Check tide times with a grown-up before exploring.

Tides are gravity dancing with spinning Earth.

Wave hello to the Moon's quiet ocean tug.

stories.title: Why Do Flowers Smell Nice?
stories.text:
A garden blossom smells sweet today.

Many flowers make scents to invite helpers.

Bees and butterflies follow smell and color.

Helpers move pollen from flower to flower.

Pollen travel helps plants make seeds.

Pretty smell is a plant's invitation card.

Not every flower smells sweet to people.

Some smells fit beetles or night moths better.

Sniff gently—do not crush the bloom.

Garden perfume is science plus kindness.

Thank the helpers that answer the scent.

Breathe in soft, smile, leave the flower be.

stories.title: Why Do Trees Need Roots?
stories.text:
Guangguang tugs a weed gently. Roots cling.

Roots anchor trees so wind doesn’t tip them. They drink water and minerals from soil and can store food. Tiny root hairs increase the drinking surface.

Healthy soil and careful watering help roots. What you see as a trunk is only half the tree’s story.

stories.title: Why Do We Recycle?
stories.text:
Bins for paper, bottles, cans.

Recycling means turning used materials into new things so we dig up and make less from scratch. It can save energy and reduce trash in landfills.

Rinse containers, follow local rules, and reuse when you can. Small habits protect the shared home called Earth.

stories.title: Why Do Mountains Form?
stories.text:
Pointy peaks. “Pushed up?”

Earth’s crust is broken into plates that slowly move. When plates collide or lift, rock can fold and rise into mountains over millions of years. Volcanoes can build mountains too.

Mountains keep growing and eroding at the same time—very slowly.

So mountains are slow-motion crumples and piles in Earth’s crust.

stories.title: What Are Fossils?
stories.text:
A stone shell print. “Dinosaur phone cases?”

Fossils are remains or traces of ancient life preserved in rock—bones, shells, footprints, even leaf prints. They form when buried remains are replaced or cast over long time.

Museums protect real fossils. Look, don’t pocket, at parks that forbid collecting.

So fossils are nature’s time capsules pressed into stone.

stories.title: Why Do Rivers Curve?
stories.text:
A snake of water. “Why not straight?”

Water erodes outer bends and drops sediment on inner bends, exaggerating curves called meanders. Over ages, loops can even cut off into oxbow lakes.

Engineers sometimes straighten channels—but curves are natural sculpture.

So river curves are water’s long habit of chewing one bank more than the other.

stories.title: What Is Soil Made Of?
stories.text:
Dirt under nails. “Just mud?”

Soil mixes mineral bits from rocks, decaying plants and animals, water, air, and countless tiny organisms. Different soils drain and feed plants differently.

Healthy soil grows food. Composting returns scraps to the cycle.

So soil is a living recipe, not lifeless dust.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Day and Night?
stories.text:
Bright then dark. “Sun switching off?”

Earth rotates. The side facing the Sun has day; the side turned away has night. The Sun stays shining—our planet’s spin creates the rhythm.

A full spin takes about 24 hours. Clocks track that turn.

So day and night are Earth’s pirouette under steady sunlight.

stories.title: What Causes Caves?
stories.text:
Echoey dark. “Hollow hills?”

Many caves form when water slowly dissolves limestone underground, carving rooms and tunnels. Rivers can cut caves too. Stalactites drip minerals from ceilings over ages.

Explore only with guides. Caves are fragile and easy to get lost in.

So caves are water’s quiet sculpture studios inside rock.

stories.title: Why Do Glaciers Move?
stories.text:
Ice that creeps. “Frozen rivers?”

Glaciers are thick snow packed into ice that slowly flows under its own weight. They carve valleys and carry rocks, reshaping land over centuries.

Climate warming makes many glaciers shrink. Scientists track them.

So glaciers are slow ice conveyors powered by gravity and thickness.

stories.title: What Is the Water Cycle?
stories.text:
Puddle → cloud → rain. “Loop?”

Water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow, flows in rivers, and soaks into ground—then repeats. You’re drinking ancient traveled water.

Saving water respects the shared loop. Pollution hitchhikes the same paths.

So the water cycle is Earth’s recycling program for H2O.

stories.title: Why Do Some Rocks Sparkle?
stories.text:
Glitter in granite. “Gem dust?”

Many rocks contain crystals like quartz or mica that reflect light. Crystal size depends on how the rock cooled or formed. Sparkle doesn’t always mean precious gems.

Leave park rocks in place. Collections need permission.

So sparkles are crystal faces saying hello to sunlight.

stories.title: What Is an Island?
stories.text:
Land in water. “How born?”

Islands can rise from volcanoes, sit on coral reefs, or be hilltops left when seas rose. Some were connected to continents long ago.

Island animals often evolve in unique ways. Visiting gently protects them.

So islands are land with a water moat—and many origin stories.

stories.title: Why Do Earthquakes Happen?
stories.text:
Rumble. Soft voice. “Why shake?”

Earth’s plates grind and stick, then slip. The sudden slip releases energy as seismic waves we feel as earthquakes. Most are small; some are strong.

Practice “drop, cover, hold on.” Kits and plans help families.

So earthquakes are stuck rocks finally sliding—prepare, don’t panic-study only.

stories.title: What Are Minerals?
stories.text:
Shiny cubes in a case. “Minerals?”

Minerals are natural solids with ordered crystal structures and definite chemistry—quartz, salt, diamond. Rocks are often mixtures of minerals.

Vitamins in food are different from rock minerals, though some elements overlap names.

So museum minerals are Earth’s crystal building blocks.

stories.title: Why Do Beaches Have Sand?
stories.text:
Toes in grit. “Where from?”

Waves and weather break rocks into smaller bits. Rivers carry grains to shores. Shells and coral add pieces too. Wind sorts and piles dunes.

Sand colors tell origin stories—black volcanic, white coral, golden quartz.

So beach sand is mountain and shell confetti tumbled by water.

stories.title: What Is Compost?
stories.text:
Brown gold in a bin. “Compost?”

Composting lets microbes break kitchen scraps and yard waste into crumbly soil helper. Air, moisture, and a mix of greens and browns keep the crew happy.

No meat or oily scraps in many home bins—follow local rules. Wash hands after.

So compost is a recycling factory run by invisible chefs.

stories.title: Why Do Trees Help the Air?
stories.text:
Shade and breath. “Trees = good air?”

Leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis. Trees also filter some dust and cool cities with shade. Forests are climate helpers when protected.

Planting the right tree in the right place matters. Forests aren’t infinite.

So trees are quiet air partners—and homes for countless creatures.

stories.title: What Is Groundwater?
stories.text:
A well pump. “Invisible rivers?”

Groundwater is water soaking through soil into spaces in rock underground. Wells tap it. It moves slowly and can stay clean if we protect the land above.

Spills can seep down. Careful farming and disposal protect drinking water.

So groundwater is a hidden sponge-ocean under our feet.

stories.title: Why Do We Need National Parks?
stories.text:
Big wild postcard. “Why parks?”

Parks protect landscapes, wildlife, and history so everyone can visit without turning them into parking lots. Rangers and rules keep trails and animals safer.

Pack out trash. Stay on paths. Parks are gifts we re-give by caring.

So national parks are shared treasure chests with hiking instructions.

stories.title: Eyes Get Tired—Time to Rest
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Eyes Get Tired—Time to Rest.

Guangguang: Max, you're staring at that screen like a statue.

Max: One more minute! Just one!

Guangguang: One minute often turns into eleven.

Guangguang: Sore eyes and fewer blinks? That's the alarm.

Max: How do I turn the alarm off?

Guangguang: Stop. Look far away. Soft blink.

Guangguang: Stand up and walk a little bit.

Max: So after this episode I stop?

Guangguang: After this episode—you stop. Say it.

Max: I stop. Then I pass Safety Theater!

Guangguang: Eye care isn't winning or losing—it's care. Rest now.

stories.title: Look Far, Then Near
stories.text:
Mia's nose nearly touches the tablet. "Too close!"

Eyes work hard when everything stays near.

Looking far lets eye muscles change focus.

Near work is fine in short friendly turns.

Then glance out a window to something distant.

Trees, clouds, or a far wall all help.

Far, then near—like a gentle stretch for eyes.

Guangguang coaches: chin up, soft blinks.

If the screen feels sticky-close, scoot back.

Rest breaks protect comfort, not just rules.

Mia practices: far tree, then tablet, smile.

Eyes happy: look far, then come back near.

stories.title: Bright Screens Need Soft Light
stories.text:
A dark room makes the screen feel like a hard spotlight.

Bright screens in black rooms tire eyes faster.

Add a soft lamp behind or beside you.

Room light should be gentle, not a glare fight.

Lower screen brightness until it feels calm.

Max tries: lamp on, brightness down, better.

Avoid watching in a pitch-black cave feeling.

Daytime near a window can be nicely balanced.

If you squint, the light mix needs a tweak.

Soft light + fair screen = kinder eyes.

Guangguang dims the glow and smiles.

Light the room softly—then enjoy the show.

stories.title: Sit Up, Don’t Bend Close
stories.text:
Mia folds like a pretzel over her book.

Bending close makes neck and eyes work harder.

Sit up with soft shoulders and a tall spine.

Bring the book or tablet up—not your nose down.

A pillow or stand can lift the screen kindly.

Feet on the floor help your whole posture.

Short wiggle breaks keep bodies happy.

Guangguang mirrors a proud sitting pose.

If you catch a slump, reset gently—no scolding.

Comfort now means easier reading later.

Sit up, soft eyes, friendly page distance.

Pretzel rest is for snacks—not for screens!

stories.title: Blink and Sip Water
stories.text:
"When did you last blink?" Max wonders.

Screens can make us forget soft blinks.

Blinking spreads a tear film like a tiny wipe.

Dry scratchy eyes often need more blinks.

Sip water—bodies and eyes like gentle sips.

Set a cozy blink-and-sip habit during play.

Look away, blink slowly three times, smile.

Guangguang counts blinks like a game.

If eyes feel sandy, tell a grown-up.

Comfort drinks and blinks are eye kindness.

Max blinks, sips, and the screen feels softer.

Blink, sip, continue—little care, big comfort.

stories.title: Outdoor Light Helps Eyes
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 6. Outdoor Light Helps Eyes.

Guangguang: Mia, the outdoors called. It misses you.
Mia: Five more levels!
Guangguang: Soft outdoor light helps eyes in ways indoor screens don't.
Mia: So go outside a bit?
Guangguang: With a grown-up plan—play outside, then screens feel better too.
Mia: Outside first. Then play.
Guangguang: That's the win.

stories.title: Hot Stove, Cool Hands
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 7. Hot Stove, Cool Hands.

Guangguang: Max, that stove is not a hand warmer.
Max: It looks shiny!
Guangguang: Hot means ouch. Cool hands stay away.
Max: So I don't touch?
Guangguang: Don't touch. Ask a grown-up. Kitchen heat is their job.
Max: Hands off. Ask first.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Knives Are for Grown-Ups
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 8. Knives Are for Grown-Ups.

Guangguang: Mia, that knife is not a magic wand.
Mia: I just want to help cut!
Guangguang: Helping is great—with grown-up tools for grown-ups.
Mia: So I wait?
Guangguang: Wait. Ask. Use kid-safe helpers they give you.
Mia: Knife stays with grown-ups.
Guangguang: Safe and helpful. Pass.

stories.title: Medicine Is Not Candy
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 9. Medicine Is Not Candy.

Guangguang: Max, those pills are not fruit snacks.
Max: But they're colorful!
Guangguang: Colorful can still be medicine. Medicine is not candy.
Max: Only if a grown-up gives it?
Guangguang: Only a trusted grown-up. Right dose, right time—never a snack raid.
Max: Not candy. Ask first.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Don’t Climb on Furniture
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 10. Don’t Climb on Furniture.

Guangguang: Mia, the bookshelf is not a mountain.
Mia: I can reach the top!
Guangguang: Climbing furniture can mean a hard fall.
Mia: So ask for help instead?
Guangguang: Ask a grown-up. Feet on the floor beat flying off a chair.
Mia: No furniture mountains.
Guangguang: Smart. Pass.

stories.title: Smoke Alarm Means Go Outside
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 11. Smoke Alarm Means Go Outside.

Guangguang: Max, that loud beep is not a game sound.
Max: It's noisy! Make it stop!
Guangguang: Smoke alarm means: get out, stay out, find a grown-up plan.
Max: Outside—not hide?
Guangguang: Outside with your grown-up. Practice the path when it's calm.
Max: Beep means go outside.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Stop, Look, Listen at Crossings
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 12. Stop, Look, Listen at Crossings.

Guangguang: Mia, the street is not a race track.
Mia: I can dash!
Guangguang: At crossings: stop, look, listen.
Mia: Stop… look… listen.
Guangguang: Then go when it's safe, with a grown-up.
Mia: No dashing. Stop look listen.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Wait for the Green Light
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 13. Wait for the Green Light.

Guangguang: Max, red means what?
Max: Go faster before it changes?
Guangguang: Nice try. Red means wait. Green means go—when clear.
Max: Wait for green.
Guangguang: Wait for the green light. Patience keeps you safe.
Max: Green light. Then walk.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Hold a Grown-Up’s Hand
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 14. Hold a Grown-Up’s Hand.

Guangguang: Mia, crossing alone is not a badge of bravery.
Mia: I'm big now!
Guangguang: Big kids still hold a grown-up's hand in busy streets.
Mia: Hand hold = safe?
Guangguang: Hand hold = safe. Together beats lost.
Mia: Hold hand. Cross together.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Bike Helmet On
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 15. Bike Helmet On.

Guangguang: Max, helmet hair is a hero look.
Max: Helmets are hot and silly!
Guangguang: Helmets protect your smart brain if you tip.
Max: So on before wheels roll?
Guangguang: Helmet on, then ride. Click it. Fit it.
Max: Helmet on. Then go.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Stay Where a Grown-Up Can See
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 16. Stay Where a Grown-Up Can See.

Guangguang: Mia, hide-and-seek in a mall is a bad sequel.
Mia: I'll be right back!
Guangguang: Stay where a grown-up can see you.
Mia: In sight—not around the corner?
Guangguang: In sight. If you get separated, find a worker or stay put as you practiced.
Mia: Stay visible.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Strangers Are Not Instant Friends
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 17. Strangers Are Not Instant Friends.

Guangguang: Max, a smile is nice. Instant best-friend? Not always.
Max: He offered candy!
Guangguang: Strangers are not instant friends. Kind can still be unknown.
Max: So I check with my grown-up?
Guangguang: Check first. Don't go. Don't take. Tell a trusted adult.
Max: Not instant friends. Ask first.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Say No and Find a Trusted Adult
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 18. Say No and Find a Trusted Adult.

Guangguang: Mia, what if a plan feels wrong in your tummy?
Mia: Be polite and stay?
Guangguang: You can say no. Then find a trusted adult.
Mia: No is allowed?
Guangguang: No is allowed. Your safety comes first. Practice the words.
Mia: Say no. Find my grown-up.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Passwords Stay Private
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 19. Passwords Stay Private.

Guangguang: Max, is your password a secret or a billboard?
Max: I told my classmate so we can share!
Guangguang: Passwords stay private. Sharing can unlock your stuff for others.
Max: Even friends?
Guangguang: Even friends. Grown-ups help if you forget—not the whole class.
Max: Password private.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Ask Before Clicking Links
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 20. Ask Before Clicking Links.

Guangguang: Mia, that shiny button says FREE PRIZE.
Mia: Tap tap!
Guangguang: Ask before clicking links. Some links are tricks.
Mia: Ask a grown-up first?
Guangguang: Ask first. If it feels rushy or weird, pause.
Mia: No surprise taps. Ask.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Wash Hands Before Eating
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 21. Wash Hands Before Eating.

Guangguang: Max, your hands visited the playground, then the sandwich?
Max: I'm starving!
Guangguang: Wash hands before eating. Soap beats invisible germ hitchhikers.
Max: Soap, rinse, then food?
Guangguang: Soap, rinse, then food. Quick and powerful.
Max: Wash first. Eat second.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Swim Only With a Grown-Up
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 22. Swim Only With a Grown-Up.

Guangguang: Mia, water is fun—and deep.
Mia: I can doggy-paddle!
Guangguang: Swim only with a grown-up watching. Water rules are not optional.
Mia: No solo swimming?
Guangguang: No solo. Grown-up eyes on. Life jackets when they say so.
Mia: Grown-up with me.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Wear Sunscreen Outside
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 23. Wear Sunscreen Outside.

Guangguang: Max, the sun is strong even when you feel fine.
Max: Sunscreen is sticky!
Guangguang: Wear sunscreen outside. Sticky now beats burn later.
Max: Put it on before play?
Guangguang: Before play. Grown-ups help with face and ears.
Max: Sunscreen on. Then run.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Tell an Adult If Something Hurts
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 24. Tell an Adult If Something Hurts.

Guangguang: Mia, brave is not silent when something hurts.
Mia: I don't want to bother anyone.
Guangguang: Tell an adult if something hurts—body or feelings.
Mia: Saying it is okay?
Guangguang: Saying it helps them help you. Early words beat big worries.
Mia: If it hurts, I tell.
Guangguang: Pass. You're Safety Theater strong.
